To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) autistic children do not demonstrate a neural response to illusory tones, 2) they do demonstrate a neural response that is not present in typically developing children and 3) that response is present at the same latency as a response to the same stimulus in adults with schizophrenia.

autistic individuals show an atypical neuromagnetic response to illusory auditory pitch, which may represent an underlying neural signature of at least some aspects of their atypical auditory processing.

auditory processing in autism and in particular with the perception of pitch.

the autistic children failed to demonstrate the ORN but did show a differential response to the dichotic pitch stimuli.

autistic children demonstrate an ORN response to the control stimuli that is comparable to typically developing controls, but fail to demonstrate an ORNs to the pitch stimuli, and demonstrate a response to the pitch stimuli not seen in the control group.

the current findings suggest that atypical auditory perception is present in at least some people with autism, but that the precise nature and underlying mechanisms of this phenomenon remain poorly understood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we found evidence for a failure of segregation in autistic children, but also for a differential processing of the pitch stimuli, which is not seen in typically developing children.
autistic children demonstrate atypical neural responses to illusory pitch, but that the magnitude of these differences is not sufficient to be considered a diagnostic marker of the condition.
atypical pitch processing in autism may be a manifestation of a generalised atypicality in the processing of temporal information.
The main takeaway from our work is that

autistic children may show atypical auditory processing, which is not necessarily associated with atypical pitch perception, but rather with the processing of pitch in the context of other auditory information.

autistic individuals have a reduced ORN response compared to controls, and that the autistic group has a significant response that was not present in controls, suggesting a potential neural signature of atypically processed pitch.
atypical auditory processing may play a more significant role in autism than previously thought.
